title: Count and Circle Worksheets for Kindergarten – Free Printable Activities
intro: Choose a small group from a larger collection. Children circle the requested number of pictures and explain how they know when to stop. Read the directions aloud and accept any selection with the correct count.
html:
Make the number you hear

Leo sees seven animal pictures. An adult asks him to circle three. He counts all seven correctly, then circles every animal. He can count the whole group, but this task asks for something different: choosing a smaller group and stopping at the requested number.

Try this together: put seven counters on a table and say, “Please give me three.” Let the child move one counter at a time while saying “one, two, three.” Stop and count the selected group to check.

On the worksheet, a circle plays the same role as moving a counter. Each circle identifies one selected object. The remaining objects stay outside the selected group.

Say the target before starting

Read the direction aloud and ask the child to repeat the requested number. They do not need to read the sentence independently. Point to the numeral as you say it, then cover other questions if the page feels busy. A child who forgets the target halfway through can look at the numeral again.

Touch one picture, say one number word, and draw one circle. Continue until the spoken count reaches the target. Counting and circling at the same time can be difficult at first. Let the child place counters on the selected pictures before using a pencil, or let an adult draw the circles the child indicates.

Count the selected pictures, not the whole group

When the child finishes, ask, “How many did you circle?” Touch only the circled pictures and count them once each. Then compare that count with the direction. There will be uncircled pictures left over on this sheet. They are supposed to remain uncircled.

If the child circles everything: return to a small collection of real objects. Ask for two objects from a group of five and move those two onto a separate mat. The goal is a group of two, not marking every object visible.

Different choices can all be correct

If the direction asks for three pictures, the child may choose the first three, the last three, or three from different positions. The positions do not change the quantity. Ask a second person to make a different group of three and compare the two selections by matching objects one to one.

The answer key circles one possible selection and labels it as an example. Do not mark a child's answer wrong because its circles are in different places. Check that exactly the requested number of distinct pictures is selected. Two circles around the same picture still select only one picture.

Keep drawing demands manageable

Leave enough room for a circle around each picture. A wobbly circle is fine when the selected object is clear. If pencil control is getting in the way, use pointing or counters to check the child's understanding first. Drawing a careful circle and choosing a quantity are related classroom skills, but they are not the same skill.

Choose a short follow-up

After one question, ask the child to build a new group with the same quantity using blocks or fingers. Then try a different target. If they need more help keeping track of objects, return to count-and-write practice. If selecting a requested number feels easy, compare the selected and unselected groups aloud without adding a new written calculation.

Each printable set has four activities. Every pictured group contains four through nine objects, and each requested number is smaller than its group. Change the numbers for another set, then print the worksheet, the example answer key, or both.
